summary: Explains why IPsec and Network Address Translation (NAT) often do not work together, and lists requirements for fixing the problems. The motivation is practical: VPNs are widely used by telecommuters, but NATs in home gateways and hotels get in the way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: NAT changes addresses in packets, while IPsec may check that those addresses remain unchanged. RFC 3715 catalogs the resulting problems and sets criteria for solutions, but does not define a solution protocol.

subtitle: Why address translation conflicts with IPsec and what compatibility proposals must support.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translation changes packet addresses and sometimes ports, which conflicts with IPsec integrity checks, IKE identification and traffic demultiplexing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo groups known incompatibilities into intrinsic NAT behavior, implementation weaknesses and helper features, then lists requirements for solutions and evaluates three existing approaches.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3715 is a requirements document, not a traversal protocol. It concludes that AH and NAT are fundamentally incompatible, so AH support is not required of a compatibility solution.

today: RFC 3715 is an Informational memo published in March 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo presents requirements rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Why NAT and IPsec Conflict
sections.content:
IPsec is commonly used for virtual private networks, including remote access to a corporate network. NATs in home gateways and hotels change addresses to share connectivity, and this can break IPsec or its key exchange.

RFC 3715 collects known incompatibilities and specifies criteria for evaluating protocol submissions. Its MUST and SHOULD language applies to capabilities a submission implements; the RFC itself does not define a traversal protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec protects traffic, while NAT changes packet addresses and ports. The memo explains where these changes conflict and what a proposed fix must support.

sections.title: Three Sources of Incompatibility
sections.content:
The memo groups the problems into intrinsic NAT behavior, common implementation weaknesses and NAT helper features. An intrinsic conflict is that AH includes IP addresses in its integrity check, so translating an address invalidates the check. TCP and UDP checksums also depend on IP addresses through a pseudo-header. ESP does not include those addresses in its integrity check.

Other problems include address-based IKE identifiers becoming inconsistent, fixed IKE ports and overlapping security-policy entries for hosts behind one NAT. Because ESP traffic is opaque to the translator, multiple hosts may also create ambiguity when incoming traffic is matched to a security association. Some NATs cannot handle ESP or AH traffic, expire mappings, or mishandle fragments; helper features that inspect IKE can create further problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Some conflicts follow directly from how NAT and IPsec work: changing an address can invalidate AH or a transport checksum. Other issues involve ports, fragments, shared NAT mappings or helper features that inspect IKE messages.

sections.title: Requirements for a Compatibility Solution
sections.content:
A solution MUST be deployable sooner than widespread IPv6 and SHOULD require changes only to hosts, not routers or NATs. It MUST support remote-worker connections through more than one NAT and secure host-to-host communication. It must also let firewall administrators use simple, static rules for IKE and IPsec traffic.

The solution MUST address thousands of telecommuters, including overlapping policy entries and incoming-packet demultiplexing. Gateways must support ESP tunnel mode and hosts must support IPsec transport mode. The memo says AH and NAT are fundamentally incompatible, and therefore AH traversal is not required. Solutions must interoperate with existing IKE and IPsec when NAT is absent and MUST NOT add security vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A solution must work through multiple NATs, scale to many remote users and fit existing IKE and IPsec systems. It must also preserve firewall controls and avoid adding new security weaknesses.

sections.title: Approaches Reviewed by the RFC
sections.content:
IPsec tunnel mode can pass through a NAT in a limited set of circumstances, including use of ESP, one client behind the NAT, suitable policy entries, no fragmentation and active traffic. The memo considers these constraints too restrictive for a general solution.

RSIP can address SPI demultiplexing and overlapping policy entries, but requires an RSIP-enabled gateway and substantial host changes. 6to4 can work when one NAT separates a client and gateway, but needs a routable IPv4 address on the NAT, does not cover multiple NATs and requires NAT support.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo reviews IPsec tunnel mode, RSIP and 6to4. Each can handle some NAT arrangements, but each has limits that keep it from meeting the full set of requirements.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
A compatibility design must process packets whose IP headers are not cryptographically protected. The memo warns that ESP with null encryption does not provide all the protections of AH. A solution MUST provide some degree of anti-spoofing protection, so a host cannot use another host's source address to gain its privileges.

RFC 3715 is an Informational requirements document. It evaluates the problem and candidate approaches but does not specify the eventual NAT traversal mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Address translation can weaken checks that depend on packet addresses. A solution must stop one host from claiming another host's address to obtain its access rights.
